Tips & Templates

WSU Hedgerow Site

When designing your hedgerow, start with circles to represent the spacing for each type/size of plant (e.g. small shrubs vs. trees) rather than the size of the plants themselves. Using the recommended spacing, the center of one tree (large, orange circles here) should be 10 feet from the center of another tree. When laying out large shrubs (medium, purple circles) in the same way, those circles should not overlap one another, but can fill in and overlap the trees’ spacing.

The spacing recommendations ensure the center of each plant is a certain distance from another—the actual plants you choose might be larger or smaller than their spacing circles.

When you drop in the actual widths of your chosen plants (we suggest using the height and width of the plant at at least around 8 years maturity), do so from the largest category to smallest in order to get a sense of what will fit. Remember, two trees spaced 10 feet apart might not require the same amount of space underneath. One could be bushy and wide near the ground, the other could have a narrow trunk and a 20-foot spread in the canopy, which will change the plants you choose to place around and under it.

Spacing guidance and diagrams from the Hedgerow Planting Templates by NPSF and Washington State University Extension.

Ready-made planting plans from the WSU Hedgerows site. Each template covers one hedgerow goal, with primary plant options for every layer plus alternatives to mix and match. These links open the files in a new tab.

Upload a CSV to fill the plant menu

Your file needs a header row with these five column names, in any order (capitalization doesn’t matter):

ColumnWhat to enter
Menu labelThe longer name shown in the plant menu
Display labelThe name shown on the circle. To use a second line, type | where it should break (for example PIN|CON), or put a real line break inside quotes.
Text sizeA number, or leave blank to auto-size to the circle
DiameterSpacing circle diameter in feet, such as 6 or 2.5
LayerTrees, Large shrubs, Small shrubs, Herbaceous, or the name of a layer you created

Colors and patterns are assigned automatically, and you can change them after adding a plant to the block plan. Plants are added to your current menu. Rows with a missing or invalid diameter or layer are skipped.

Menu label,Display label,Text size,Diameter,Layer

Snowberry (deciduous with berries),Snowberry,12,4,Small shrubs

Presets

Tick the plants to add to your Add a plant menu. Hold Shift and click to tick a run of plants at once. Plants already in the menu are greyed out. Lists you save with Save plant list appear under User presets.

About

The Native Plant Salvage Project was started in 1994 to involve Thurston County residents in direct action to protect water resources and improve habitat. Our mission is to provide hands-on education to protect and conserve water resources and habitat from the South Sound prairies to the shores of the Salish Sea.

What’s new and what’s changed in the planner, newest first.

November 7, 2026 update

  • Fixed: pressing Delete sometimes didn’t remove the selected circle after you’d been editing a label or ticking a setting.
  • In the spacing diagram, the key now shows how many of each plant are on the block plan inside its color swatch, and the swatches use a finer pattern so dots and stripes are easy to see. The planting diagram key still shows the count after the name.
  • More options has a new Display options group with a “Show common names in key” switch. It’s off to start, so the key lists plants by scientific name; turn it on to include common names.
  • Presets now has a “By plant characteristic” section under the Native Plant Salvage Foundation, with lists such as Pollinator-attracting, Larval hosts and Soil-binding, so you can pick plants by what they do in a hedgerow.
  • Loading a saved layout now offers to add any of its plants that aren’t in your Add a plant menu, so you can place more of them and update them later.
